newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany marks Unity Day amid divisions.
newsitem.headline: Germany marks Unity Day amid divisions.

text.p: Germany marked the anniversary of its unification on Thursday with calls to break down the human barriers of intolerance that remained when the Berlin Wall fell.

Militant left- and right-wingers, however, garnered little support despite six years of economic turmoil and uncertainty that have followed unification. Some 400 militant left-wingers protested in Munich under the banner "There's nothing to celebrate" and 100 skinheads and neo-Nazis marched in Bonn.
Parliamentary speaker Rita Suessmuth told guests at Munich's sumptuous Residence, once the seat of Bavaria's Wittelsbacher royal dynasty:
"Our central problem is a mental one. We need to change the way we think and behave."

The former East Germany has suffered serious unemployment as outdated and uncompetitive factories have been shut down. This has come as a bitter blow to people who had learnt to expect job security, in return for political passivity.
Some west Germans, in turn, have come to resent vast subsidies paid to revive eastern Germany, seeing them as a threat to economic strength they have enjoyed since the 1950s.
In a speech at official Unity Day celebrations, Suessmuth said east Germans had suffered the "culture shock" of being plunged into a new system after four decades of Communist rule.
But she acknowledged that west Germans had also struggled to adapt to unification.
"It would help if more West Germans would visit and become acquainted with the other part of Germany, which has had a different historical and human development," she said.

A recent survey showed rather than beginning to feel closer, 29 percent of west Germans and 57 percent of east Germans said they felt more alienated from each other six years after German unification on October 3, 1990.
Moreover, only 562 of 16,383 weddings in 1995 brought together partners from the formerly communist east and west Berlin, a democratic enclave once surrounded by East Germany.
Partners from east and west were keener to marry foreigners rather than marry across the former Cold War divide.

"There are citizens who think our state is still divided, despite the fact the Berlin Wall and its barbed wire have long disappeared," Berlin's mayor Eberhard Diepgen told guests at Unity day celebrations in Berlin's Schauspielhaus theatre.
"They will have to realise the east and west now belong together," he said in a speech.
Diepgen criticised those who use the pejorative terms "Ossie" -- used by west Germans to describe east Germans and "Wessie" -- used by east Germans to describe west Germans.
"By using these words people do not serve unity. They are divisive -- often without intending to be," he said.

Police said 150 supporters of the extreme rightist National Democratic Party of Germany held a rally in Bonn and that hundreds of police had to form a human barrier to prevent them clashing with 300 left-wingers staying a counter-demonstration.
In Munich, Suessmuth hailed her guest of honour Hungary's Prime Minister Gyula Horn and thanked him for his part in the unification process.

Horn gave orders to open the border in 1989 from his country to Austria sparking a mass exodus of East Germans to the West. The move led, through mass demonstrations at home, to unification a year later.
